# MDR Software Classification: infusion pump rate control app (tablet)

**Intended purpose (as stated):** "to set and adjust the delivery rate of the [X] infusion pump under clinician control."
**Qualified as a device:** assumed — but see the note below on whether it's a device in its own right or part of the pump

## Class: III

**Route:** 3.3 → drives a device → same class as the driven device (the pump, Class III). Rule 11 is not reached.

## Reasoning

| Step | Question | Answer | Basis |
|---|---|---|---|
| 3.1 | Intended purpose | "to set and adjust the delivery rate of the [X] infusion pump under clinician control" | `[verified]` |
| 3.3 | Drives or influences another device? | **Yes** — setting and adjusting the delivery rate is driving the pump, not merely displaying its output | `[verified]` |
| 3.3 | Consequence | Falls within the same class as that device → **III** | `[verified]` |
| Rule 11 | Which limb | **Not reached** — 3.3 governs first and only independent software is classified in its own right | `[verified]` |
| Rule 11 | Escalation | n/a | `[verified]` |
| 3.5 | Could a stricter rule apply? | No — III is the highest class; nothing can raise it | `[verified]` |

The "it doesn't diagnose anything" point is a Rule 11 argument, and Rule 11 is never reached here. 3.3 runs first: software that drives a device takes that device's class regardless of what Rule 11 would have said on its own. The rate-display function doesn't change this — display alone would point toward independence, but the same software sets the parameter, and 3.1 classifies on the intended purpose as a whole, which is the setting and adjusting.

"Under clinician control" also doesn't pull it out of 3.3. A clinician deciding the number does not stop the software from being what transmits and applies it to the pump.

## What would change this

- **If the app did not set or adjust anything** — pure remote display of the pump's current rate, with no path to change it. That would be a genuine 3.3 independence question, and Rule 11 would then apply. As stated, it isn't.
- **The pump's actual class.** Your answer is pinned to it. If the pump is Class III, the app is III; if the pump were reclassified, the app moves with it.
- **How the intended purpose is written.** If the technical documentation states something broader than the sentence you gave me — dose calculation, regimen suggestion, alarm handling — that's a different analysis, and it's worth checking that the written purpose matches what the app does.

## One prior question worth naming

There's a step before class here that I can't settle: whether this app is a **device in its own right** (or an accessory) versus a **component of the pump system** placed on the market as part of the pump. If it's the latter, it isn't separately classified at all — it's covered by the pump's own conformity assessment and technical documentation. Either way it sits in a Class III conformity route, but which one determines whether you need separate CE marking, a separate UDI, and separate documentation. That's an Art. 2(1) / product-structure question this skill doesn't carry `[verify]`.

## Before you build on this

This is the Annex VIII text applied to the intended purpose as you stated it. The class drives your conformity route, whether you need a notified body, and the depth of your technical documentation, so it should be confirmed by your regulatory lead or notified body before you build on it. The three things to put in front of them:

1. The **3.3 call** — the app drives the pump, so it takes the pump's class rather than being classified under Rule 11.
2. **No Rule 11 limb or escalation applies**, because 3.3 resolves it first.
3. **No 3.5 question** — III is the ceiling.

Plus the component-versus-standalone-device question above, which changes the paperwork rather than the class.

## Limits

> This classifies software under MDR Annex VIII implementing rules 3.1–3.7 and Rule 11, retrieved verbatim from EUR-Lex on 2026-09-09. It does **not** cover Art. 2(1) qualification, Rules 1–10 or 12–22, Annex XVI, IVDR, MDCG guidance, notified-body practice, or national interpretation. Rule 11 is a floor: under 3.5 a stricter rule this skill does not carry may raise the class. A structured first pass and an audit aid, not legal or regulatory advice, and not a substitute for your notified body or a qualified regulatory professional.

## Class III — it inherits the pump's class

The operative provision is **MDR Annex VIII, Chapter II, implementing rule 3.3**:

> Software, which drives a device or influences the use of a device, shall fall within the same class as the device. If the software is independent of any other device, it shall be classified in its own right.

Your app sets the delivery rate on the pump. That is "drives a device" in the most literal sense available — your own intended purpose statement names the pump explicitly, so there's no reading in which this software is independent. Same class as the pump: **III**. MDCG 2019-11 uses essentially this example (software controlling an infusion pump) to illustrate the rule.

**Why "it doesn't diagnose anything" doesn't help you.** That argument is aimed at Rule 11, which grades software by the seriousness of the decision it informs — and it's the usual route to arguing Class IIa. But you never reach Rule 11. The implementing rules in Chapter II are applied before the classification rules in Chapter III, and 3.3 disposes of the question. Rule 11 only governs software that is independent of any other device.

## The real decision: module vs. separate device

Both land on Class III rigor, but the paperwork differs a lot:

- **Component/module of the pump system.** The app is part of the pump device, covered by the pump's existing certificate and technical documentation. No separate conformity assessment. Usually much cheaper when you own both sides, which you do.
- **Separate device (or accessory) placed on the market in its own right.** Its own technical documentation, its own Class III conformity assessment — which means notified body examination of the design dossier — and its own UDI-DI.

The question your notified body will press on: is the app ever distributed, labelled, versioned, or updated independently of the pump? If yes, you're closer to the second path whether you intended it or not. Tablet-app distribution via an app store tends to push you there.

## Don't conflate this with IEC 62304

Different axis. MDR Class III doesn't mechanically make you software safety Class C, but for a UI whose sole job is setting an infusion rate, **C is the default expectation**. You can argue B only if the risk analysis shows pump-side protections independent of the app — hard rate ceilings, drug-library limits, an independent watchdog that rejects out-of-range commands. Worth establishing that architecture early; it's the single biggest lever on your software documentation burden.

## Two other things this pulls in

- **Annex I §17** (electronic programmable systems) applies, including §17.4: you must specify minimum hardware, OS versions, and IT characteristics for the tablet. Off-the-shelf tablets mean OS auto-updates are a risk control problem you have to address explicitly, not a deployment detail.
- **The link to the pump is safety-critical.** If it's wireless, loss, delay, or corruption of a rate command is a top-level hazard, and cybersecurity documentation per MDCG 2019-16 is expected.

## One caveat on the premise

The class is inherited, so it's only as correct as the pump's classification. Rule 12 puts devices administering medicines at IIb, reaching III only where the manner of administration is potentially hazardous. If the pump's Class III determination is sound, you're at III; if it's actually IIb, your app is IIb. Worth confirming the pump's rationale rather than assuming it.

This is my read of the regulation, not a regulatory opinion — get it confirmed by your RA function or notified body before it goes in the technical file.

## Class III

Under **MDR Annex VIII, Chapter II (Implementing Rules), rule 3.3**:

> "Software, which drives a device or influences the use of a device, shall fall within the same class as the device."

Your app sets and adjusts the delivery rate — that is the textbook definition of *driving* the pump. So it inherits the pump's class: **III**.

### Why the arguments you raised don't move it

- **"It doesn't diagnose anything."** Irrelevant here. Rule 11 (the diagnostic/therapeutic-information software rule) applies to software that's *independent* of another device. Yours isn't — rule 3.3 governs and pre-empts it. There's no path where "no diagnostic claim" gets you to IIa.
- **"Under clinician control."** Human-in-the-loop has no downgrading effect under rule 3.3. The clinician sets a number; your software is what transmits it to a Class III pump.
- **"It's just a display."** Displaying the current rate is part of influencing use, and in any case the whole product is classified together under the strictest applicable rule (rule 3.5).

MDCG 2019-11 confirms this reading explicitly for driving/influencing software, including when it's an accessory.

### The real decision: separate device vs. part of the pump

Both end at Class III, but the regulatory mechanics differ a lot:

1. **Component of the pump system** — covered by the pump's own technical documentation, UDI and certificate. Cleaner paperwork, but every significant app change flows through the pump's change control and notified-body notification. That's painful if you want normal app release cadence.
2. **Placed on the market in its own right** (separate UDI-DI, own certificate as Class III standalone software) — more artefacts to maintain, but the app's lifecycle is decoupled from the pump's.

Most teams underestimate how much option 1 slows releases. Worth deciding early, because it shapes your technical documentation structure.

### What Class III pulls in

- Annex IX conformity assessment: notified body QMS audit **plus** per-device technical documentation assessment.
- Clinical investigation presumed required under Art. 61(4), unless you can rely on the modification/equivalence exemption for an already-marketed device of your own.
- SSCP (Art. 32), annual PSUR submitted to the notified body, enhanced PMCF.
- Not subject to the Art. 54 scrutiny/expert-panel procedure — that's for Class III *implantables* and Class IIb active devices administering medicinal products. Your software isn't implantable.

Separately and often confused: **IEC 62304 software safety classification is not the MDR class.** Given a wrong rate can cause death or serious injury, expect **Class C** — but derive it from your ISO 14971 hazard analysis, including whether pump-side hardware limits (rate ceilings, occlusion/dose-error reduction) are independent enough to count as external risk controls.

### One thing to verify

You've stated the pump is Class III. Since your app's class is entirely parasitic on that, it's worth confirming the pump's own classification is right — infusion pumps land in IIb under Rule 12 by default and only reach III when the mode of administration is potentially hazardous (PCA, epidural/intrathecal, neonatal, high-risk drugs). If the pump is actually IIb, your app is IIb. If you tell me the drug/route, I can sanity-check the Rule 12 call.

graders.name: criteria
graders.evidence:
**Class III.** The same class as the pump.

## Why

MDR Annex VIII, Chapter II, implementing rule 3.3:

> "Software, which drives a device or influences the use of a device, shall fall within the same class as the device. If the software is independent of any other device, it shall be classified in its own right."

Your app sets the delivery rate. That is the textbook case of software that *drives* a device — it's not merely adjacent to the pump, it commands its therapeutic output. So it inherits Class III and never reaches a classification rule of its own.

This is also how MDCG 2019-11 (qualification and classification of software under MDR/IVDR) treats it: the "drives or influences" branch is decided before you ever get to the MDSW rules, and control of an infusion pump is the canonical example.

## The "it doesn't diagnose anything" point doesn't help you

That argument is aimed at Rule 11, which classifies software *intended to provide information used to take decisions for diagnostic or therapeutic purposes*. Rule 11 only applies to software that is independent of any other device. Yours isn't, so Rule 11 is simply not the operative rule — and rule 3.3 gets you to III regardless. (Even if Rule 11 did apply, incorrect infusion rates can cause death or irreversible deterioration, so it would land on Class III too. And per implementing rule 3.5, when several rules apply you take the strictest.)

The same goes for "it just shows the current rate." Displaying the rate is part of the control loop the clinician relies on; it doesn't create a separate, lower-risk claim.

## One structural decision worth making deliberately

Since you make the pump as well, you have a choice:

1. **Ship the app as part of the pump.** It goes into the pump's technical documentation and CE certificate as a component of the system. Usually the lower-overhead path — no separate device registration, no separate UDI-DI, one clinical evaluation.
2. **Ship it as a standalone accessory.** Accessories are classified in their own right (Art. 51(1) / Annex VIII 3.2), but rule 3.3 still lands it at Class III. You'd get its own UDI, its own declaration of conformity, its own entry in EUDAMED.

Pick (2) only if you actually need to place it on the market or version it independently of the pump. Either way the class is III and a notified body is involved (Annex IX Chapters I+II, or Annex X + XI Part A). Article 54 scrutiny doesn't apply — that's for Class III *implantables* and Class IIb actives for administering medicinal products — but the pump itself may be caught by it, so check that separately.

## Two things to verify and three to plan for

**Verify:** that the pump is genuinely Class III *under MDR*, not carried over from an MDD Class IIb certificate. Annex VIII Rule 12 puts medicine-administering devices at IIb unless the manner of application is potentially hazardous, in which case III. Your app's class moves with whatever the answer is. Also confirm nothing in the app adds a function beyond rate control (dose calculation, drug libraries with limits, alarms) — those change the clinical claim, not the class, but they change the evidence you need.

**Plan for:** IEC 62304 software safety Class C (separate from the MDR class, but a wrong rate can kill, so it's C); IEC 62366-1 usability engineering with summative validation, which for a rate-entry UI is where notified bodies will focus hardest; and, if the app runs on an off-the-shelf tablet, a defined computing platform with minimum specs, plus a serious look at IEC 60601-1-8 if it annunciates any alarm condition — a consumer tablet that can silence itself, run out of battery, or lose Bluetooth is a well-known review flashpoint.

This is my read of the regulation, not a regulatory opinion — run the accessory-vs-component decision past your notified body before you commit, since it shapes the whole submission.

# MDR Software Classification: CTA large-vessel-occlusion triage software

**Intended purpose (as stated):** *"to provide information triage information to support the decision to proceed to mechanical thrombectomy in suspected acute ischaemic stroke."*

**Qualified as a device:** not established by anything you've given me — see note below. The classification below assumes it is.

## Class: III

**Route:** 3.3 independent → Rule 11 limb 1 → escalation on the first indent (death or irreversible deterioration)

## Reasoning

| Step | Question | Answer | Basis |
|---|---|---|---|
| 3.1 | Intended purpose | *"to provide triage information to support the decision to proceed to mechanical thrombectomy in suspected acute ischaemic stroke"* | `[verified]` |
| 3.3 | Drives or influences another device? | No. Standalone, no connection to any other device. It consumes CTA images but does not drive the scanner or influence how it is operated → classified in its own right | `[verified]` |
| Rule 11 | Which limb | Limb 1 — information used to take decisions with diagnosis or therapeutic purposes. Base class **IIa** | `[verified]` |
| Rule 11 | Escalation | **III.** A wrong decision may cause death or irreversible deterioration: a missed LVO means thrombectomy is not performed, and the consequence is infarct progression — irreversible neurological deficit or death. The IIb indent is *also* engaged (the decision is whether to proceed to a surgical intervention), but 3.5 takes the stricter sub-rule | `[verified]` |
| 3.5 | Could a stricter rule apply? | No — III is the highest class, so nothing this skill doesn't carry can raise it further | `[verified]` |

The escalation here is unusually clean because **both** indents of limb 1 fire independently. The decision the output feeds is literally a decision to perform surgery (IIb), and the harm from getting it wrong in either direction is irreversible (III). You don't need the borderline reasoning about stroke severity — 3.5 resolves it to III on the text.

## Two things worth flagging

**"Triage information to support the decision" does not soften limb 1.** Limb 1 asks whether the software provides information *used to take* a diagnostic or therapeutic decision. It does not require the software to be decisive, and it does not carve out an exception for a human in the loop. The neurointerventionalist reviewing the images themselves is a risk control, not a classification argument. If you intend to argue that the human reader moderates the class, that argument runs through MDCG 2019-11, which is Commission guidance rather than the regulation and which I do not verify. The Annex VIII text takes me to III. I can flag the guidance question, or you can point me at the passage.

**Qualification is a prior question I haven't settled.** Classification presumes the product is a medical device under Art. 2(1), which this skill does not carry. On your description it plainly looks like one, but I am not stating that as a finding — if it is already established in your documentation, the class above stands; if it isn't, that comes first.

## What would change this

## Qualification first

It's a medical device. Standalone software with a diagnostic purpose falls under Article 2(1) MDR, and it satisfies the MDCG 2019-11 decision steps: it performs an action on data beyond storage/communication/simple search (image analysis, LVO detection) and does so for the benefit of an individual patient. Not Annex XVI, not an IVD (it acts on images, not specimens).

Because it's independent of any other device, Annex VIII §3.3 means it's classified in its own right — it does not inherit the class of the CT scanner.

## Rule 11, first indent → **Class III**

Rule 11 is *lex specialis* for software and displaces Rule 10 here. The chain:

- The software **provides information used to take decisions with diagnostic or therapeutic purposes** → baseline Class IIa.
- Escalation turns entirely on the *impact of the decision the information feeds*. For LVO stroke that decision is thrombectomy vs. no thrombectomy, and the failure modes are:
  - **False negative / missed or delayed LVO** → no thrombectomy, or thrombectomy outside the window. The consequence is permanent infarction: irreversible deterioration or death.
  - **False positive** → an unnecessary catheter-based neurointervention, which itself carries a mortality and major-stroke risk.

The first indent ("death or an irreversible deterioration of a person's state of health") is met, so it goes to **Class III**, not IIb. Annex VIII §3.2 (strictest applicable rule) confirms you can't settle for the IIb "surgical intervention" indent when the irreversible-harm indent also bites.

## On the III vs IIb argument you'll hear

Manufacturers do argue IIb on two grounds; both are weak on your facts.

1. *"There's a clinician in the loop — the neurointerventionalist reads the images anyway."* Rule 11 already presupposes a human decision-maker; that's what "information which is used to take decisions" means. Notified bodies have consistently declined to treat human review as a downgrade factor.
2. *"It's only triage."* This is the one that actually matters, and it's a drafting question, not a technical one. Your stated intended purpose explicitly binds the output to *"the decision to proceed to mechanical thrombectomy."* That is driving clinical management of an individual patient. A genuinely narrower claim — worklist prioritisation, with no LVO determination and no link to the treatment decision — is a different device with a different risk profile. You cannot write that claim and then market this one; the labelling, promotional material and clinical evidence all have to match, and a notified body will read them together.

So: **Class III as specified.** If IIb is commercially necessary, that's a product and intended-purpose decision to take now, before the clinical evidence strategy is locked — not a classification argument to win later.

## What Class III pulls in

- **Notified body conformity assessment**: Annex IX (QMS + assessment of the technical documentation for the device), or Annex X + XI as the alternative route.
- **Article 61(4)**: clinical investigations are *required* for Class III devices unless you fit an exemption — most relevantly demonstrated equivalence to an already-marketed device under Annex XIV Part A §3, which requires contractual access to the comparator's full technical documentation. In practice for a novel AI triage tool, plan for a clinical investigation.
- **Article 32**: Summary of Safety and Clinical Performance (SSCP), validated by the NB.
- **PSUR** updated annually and submitted to the NB via Eudamed (Art. 86); PMCF plan and evaluation report.
- **No CECP**. Article 54 clinical evaluation consultation applies to Class III *implantable* devices and certain Class IIb actives — software isn't caught.
- **IEC 62304 safety Class C**, on the same hazard reasoning. Note this is derived independently of the MDR class, but lands in the same place.
- **AI Act**: if it's ML-based, it is a high-risk AI system under Article 6(1) — it's a safety component of a product requiring third-party conformity assessment under an Annex I harmonised act. ## Verdict: Class III under Rule 11

Here's the reasoning chain.

### 1. Qualification — it is a medical device

Article 2(1) MDR: software with an intended purpose of diagnosis, prediction or prognosis of disease qualifies in its own right. Applying the MDCG 2019-11 decision steps: it performs an action on data beyond storage, archiving, communication or simple search (it analyses CTA images and creates new information), and it does so for the benefit of individual patients. So it's MDSW, not a mere PACS/viewer accessory. Note also Article 2(4) — software is deemed an **active device**.

### 2. Which rule applies

Annex VIII implementing rule 3.3: software independent of any other device is classified in its own right. Your product is standalone, so you don't inherit the class of a CT scanner or anything else.

Rule 11 is the operative rule. Rule 10 (active devices for diagnosis) is displaced here — Rule 11 is the lex specialis for software, and implementing rule 3.5 would in any case push you to the strictest applicable rule/sub-rule.

### 3. Rule 11, first limb

The device "provides information which is used to take decisions with diagnosis or therapeutic purposes" → baseline IIa, escalated by the impact of those decisions:

- **Irreversible deterioration or death → Class III**
- **Serious deterioration or a surgical intervention → Class IIb**

Both failure directions are in scope here, and implementing rule 3.5 means the strictest sub-rule wins:

- **False negative:** LVO missed or de-prioritised, thrombectomy not performed or performed outside the window. Untreated LVO stroke is the textbook case of irreversible deterioration — permanent disability or death. This is the Class III limb, squarely.
- **False positive:** patient taken to an unnecessary endovascular procedure. That is at minimum "a surgical intervention" (IIb limb), and thrombectomy itself carries a risk of dissection, perforation and haemorrhagic death, so it can reach the III limb too.

So: **Class III.**

### 4. The Class IIb argument, and why I don't think it holds

The wording you've drafted — *"triage information to support the decision"* — is clearly aiming at a human-in-the-loop / adjunctive framing: the neurointerventionalist reads the CTA independently, the software only prioritises the worklist, therefore the software doesn't *drive* the decision and the residual impact is "surgical intervention" at worst → IIb.

Two problems with that. First, Rule 11 asks about the impact of *the decision the information is used to take*, not about whether the software is the sole input. If clinician oversight downgraded the class, essentially no MDSW would ever be Class III, which is plainly not the intent — notified bodies have converged on this reading. Second, the argument is self-defeating for a triage product specifically: the entire value proposition is that the case might otherwise sit unread in the queue, so a suppressed alert isn't neutral, it costs time in a pathway where time is brain.

You could try to negotiate to IIb by rewriting the intended purpose as pure notification/prioritisation with no diagnostic claim ("notifies the on-call team of the presence of a suspected LVO; not intended to be used as the basis for a diagnosis or treatment decision"), plus mandatory independent review before any action. Be aware that this constrains your labelling, your clinical claims and your marketing, and that a notified body will test whether real-world use matches it. Given your stated purpose as written, I'd plan for III.

### 5. What Class III costs you

The practical stakes of the III/IIb line are large, which is why it's worth getting right up front rather than at the application:

- **Conformity assessment:** Annex IX (full QMS *plus* technical documentation assessment of **every** device), or Annex X type-examination + Annex XI Part A. Under IIb the NB samples technical documentation on a representative basis per generic device group instead.
- **Clinical investigation:** Article 61(4) requires one for Class III devices, with narrow exemptions (essentially modification of your own already-marketed device, or legacy data under Art 61(6)). For a novel product this means a prospective study, and it's usually the dominant cost and schedule driver.
- **SSCP:** Article 32 — required for Class III, not for IIb.
- **PSUR:** annual update, submitted to the NB via Eudamed for Class III.

Article 54 scrutiny / expert panel does **not** apply — that's limited to Class III *implantable* and Class IIb active devices administering or removing medicinal products.

### 6. Adjacent obligations to line up now

- **EU AI Act:** this is high-risk under Article 6(1) — an AI system that is a safety component of a product subject to third-party conformity assessment under MDR (Annex I Section A). Chapter III obligations apply, via a combined conformity assessment with your notified body, from **2 August 2027**. Design the technical file so the MDR and AI Act evidence share one backbone rather than being bolted together later.
- **IEC 62304 software safety class C** — same "death or serious injury" logic as the classification.
- **GSPR Annex I, Chapter 17** for electronic programmable systems, plus ISO 14971, IEC 62366-1 and IEC 82304-1.

One aside in case it's an anchor for you: in the US this category (computer-aided triage, CADt) typically clears as Class II via De Novo/510(k). That divergence is real and is not a signal that the MDR answer should be lower.

## Short answer

If it qualifies as a medical device at all, it's **Class IIa under MDR Annex VIII, Rule 11**. The genuinely contested question here isn't the class — it's whether "trending" pushes you over the qualification threshold in the first place. Plan for IIa unless you deliberately engineer the product to stay out of scope.

## Step 1 — is it MDSW? (this is the real decision)

Two things in your intended purpose pull in opposite directions.

**Toward out-of-scope:** MDCG 2019-11's decision step asks whether the software performs *an action on data beyond storage, archival, communication, simple search or lossless compression*. A plain chart of the raw values the patient typed in is arguably just display of stored data — an electronic logbook. Logbooks/diaries are not devices.

**Toward MDSW:** your stated purpose is explicitly clinical — CKD patients, review by a nephrologist. Weight and BP trends in CKD *are* the fluid-status and hypertension-control signal the nephrologist titrates against. MDR Art. 2(1) covers software with a purpose of **monitoring** of disease, and the EU has no clinical-decision-support carve-out equivalent to the US Cures Act. "No alarms, not acute" reduces risk; it does not remove medical purpose.

The hinge is what *trend* actually means in your code:

- Plots the entered points on a time axis, nothing derived → credible non-device argument.
- Computes anything: rolling averages, slope/rate of change, % change from baseline, "dry weight" deltas, colour bands, reference ranges, highlighting outliers → you've created new medical information. That's MDSW, full stop.

Most products that market themselves as "trending" land in the second bucket.

## Step 2 — Rule 11 applies, and it gives IIa

Both limbs of Rule 11 reach the same place:

- *Information used to take decisions with diagnosis or therapeutic purposes* — the nephrologist adjusts antihypertensives or fluid targets off the trend → **IIa** by default.
- *Monitoring of physiological processes* → **IIa**.

Why not higher: the IIb/III escalations turn on the consequence of the decision (serious deterioration / surgery, or death / irreversible deterioration) and, for the monitoring limb, on variations causing *immediate danger*. Once-daily home readings reviewed weeks later at a scheduled appointment, with no alarms and no acute use, don't meet either. BP is a vital physiological parameter, but the "immediate danger" qualifier is what triggers IIb and your use case doesn't hit it.

Why not Class I: "all other software" is the residual bucket for device software that neither informs decisions nor monitors. That's a narrow set, and you're not in it.

## What I'd actually do

Pick a lane rather than drifting:

**Lane A — stay out of scope.** Strip derived computation. Reword the intended purpose to a record-and-display claim ("records and displays patient-entered values"; drop "trend", drop "for review during consultations"). Make no clinical claim anywhere in labelling, store listing, or marketing. Document the qualification rationale against MDCG 2019-11 and hold it in a file — that assessment is the deliverable a competent authority will ask for. Be honest with yourself about whether the product still has a reason to exist under this constraint; often it doesn't.

**Lane B — accept IIa.** Class IIa means a **notified body**: ISO 13485 QMS, IEC 62304 (Class A or B software safety class — probably A given no injury pathway, but justify it), ISO 14971, IEC 62366-1 usability (transcription error on manual entry is your headline hazard), clinical evaluation per Annex XIV + MDCG 2020-1, PMS/PMCF, UDI, EUDAMED. Budget 12–18 months.

One note either way: the app not being connected to a BP cuff doesn't help your classification, and it doesn't fully offload the risk — manual entry of a misread or mistyped value is squarely your risk file, not the cuff manufacturer's.

If this is also going to UK or US markets, the answers differ — UKCA still runs on the old MDD-style rules where this plausibly lands Class I, and FDA would likely treat it as MDDS-adjacent. Say the word if you want that mapped out.

## Bottom line

Two defensible outcomes, and no middle ground: either **not a medical device at all**, or **Class IIa under Rule 11**. Class I is effectively not available. Which one you land on turns entirely on what "trend" means in code.

## Step 1 — qualification, before classification

Run MDCG 2019-11's decision tree. The gate that decides this case is step 3: *does the software perform an action on data beyond storage, archival, communication, simple search, or lossless compression?*

As described — the patient types in two numbers, the app stores them and draws them on a time axis — the answer is no. It creates no new medical information; the nephrologist derives the clinical meaning from raw values, exactly as they would from a paper diary. That makes it an electronic logbook, outside the Article 2(1) definition, notwithstanding that the users have CKD and the data is reviewed clinically. The "no alarms, not used for acute decisions" framing supports this, though it isn't itself the deciding factor.

Note that the wellness/lifestyle carve-out does **not** help you here — you've named a disease population. The "no action on data" gate is your only route to non-device status, so it has to hold cleanly.

## What flips it into a device

Any of these, and step 3 is answered "yes":

- computing a slope, moving average, % change, or weekly delta
- comparing readings against a target, threshold, or reference band (including colour-coding a graph green/amber/red)
- flagging, highlighting, or annotating readings
- any dry-weight or fluid-status inference

Plain plotting of the entered points is display. Anything that transforms them is analysis.

## Step 2 — if it is MDSW, Rule 11

Annex VIII Rule 11, first limb: software providing information used to take **diagnostic or therapeutic decisions** is **Class IIa**, escalating only where those decisions could cause death or irreversible deterioration (III) or serious deterioration / surgical intervention (IIb).

BP and weight trends in CKD feed antihypertensive and fluid-management decisions, so the first limb bites → **IIa**. It doesn't escalate: decisions are made at scheduled appointments by a specialist with full clinical context, and the app is one input among many, not the trigger for an acute intervention.

Rule 11's second limb (monitoring physiological processes) gives the same answer. BP is a vital physiological parameter, but IIb requires variations that could result in *immediate danger* — once-daily home readings reviewed weeks later don't.

And the "all other software is Class I" residual is genuinely residual under MDR. Practically nothing patient-facing and disease-specific survives in it. So IIa means a notified body, which is the real commercial consequence of getting step 1 wrong.

## Recommendation

Write and freeze the qualification rationale against MDCG 2019-11 step 3 now, with a feature list stating explicitly what the software does *not* compute. Then treat that list as a design constraint — the classification is one sprint away from changing, and a "helpful" amber threshold added later silently converts a non-device into a IIa device.

Your stated intended purpose is well-drafted for the non-device position; keep marketing, app-store copy and screenshots aligned with it (Article 7), since claims are assessed alongside the intended purpose.

Worth having a notified body or regulatory consultant confirm the step 3 call before launch — this is a known borderline area and national authorities have not always read "trending" the same way.

## Bottom line

**Class IIa under MDR Rule 11**, assuming it qualifies as a medical device at all — and with the intended purpose as you've written it, it does. There is a narrow, defensible argument for "not a medical device," but not with that wording.

## Qualification (is it a device?)

Two tests from MDCG 2019-11:

1. **Medical purpose?** Yes. The intended purpose names a disease population (CKD) and a clinical use (review during nephrology consultations). That's "monitoring" in the Art. 2(1) sense. If it said "general wellness journal," you'd be somewhere else — but it doesn't.
2. **Action beyond storage/archival/communication/simple search?** This is where it turns. Pure storage and playback of the numbers as entered is *not* a device. But "trends the readings over weeks" is the problem word. If the trend is a computed output — moving average, regression slope, rate of change, projected direction — you've created new information and you're a device. If it's literally just the raw points plotted on a time axis with no derived quantity, that's arguably presentation of stored data only.

In practice, notified bodies read the intended-purpose statement first and the algorithm second. "For review during scheduled nephrology consultations" tells them the output is meant to inform clinical management of that patient. That closes the non-device path.

## Classification (Rule 11, Annex VIII)

Rule 11 gives you two independent hooks, and you're caught by both:

- **Information for diagnostic/therapeutic decisions** → IIa. Weight and BP trends in CKD drive fluid-status assessment and diuretic/antihypertensive titration. The nephrologist is using your output to decide.
- **Monitoring physiological processes** → IIa. Trending BP over weeks is monitoring, almost by definition.

**Not IIb**, and this is worth stating explicitly in your classification rationale: BP is a vital physiological parameter, but the IIb escalation requires that variations "could result in immediate danger." Once-daily home entry, retrospective review at a scheduled appointment, no alarms, no acute use — none of that is immediate-danger monitoring. Document that reasoning; it's the argument that keeps you off IIb.

**Not III** — no death-or-irreversible-deterioration decision pathway.

Rule 3.3 of Annex VIII confirms you classify in your own right since you're standalone.

## The Class I trap

Don't expect to land on Class I. Under MDR, Rule 11 leaves Class I only for software that neither informs diagnostic/therapeutic decisions nor monitors physiological processes — scheduling, billing, general record-keeping. Products like this were Class I under MDD and got up-classified; that's the well-known Rule 11 effect. Your choice is realistically **IIa or non-device**, not IIa or I.

## If you want to pursue non-device

It's viable but requires changing the product, not just the paperwork:

- Rewrite the intended purpose as a patient-held diary with no clinical-management claim and no reference to the consultation.
- Display only the values exactly as entered. No derived trend line, no averages, no slope, no colour coding, no reference ranges or thresholds.
- No claims about CKD in labelling, store listing, or marketing. Marketing material counts as intended-purpose evidence.

If the clinician review is the actual point of the product — and it reads like it is — this path costs you the feature and I wouldn't take it.

## What IIa means for you

Notified body involvement (Annex IX Ch. I+III, or Annex XI), ISO 13485 QMS, ISO 14971 risk management, IEC 62304 (likely software safety class A given no alarms and no acute use — argue it), IEC 62366-1 usability, clinical evaluation per Annex XIV, PMS/PMCF plan, UDI, and an EU authorised rep if you're not EU-established.

One flag: data-entry error is your main hazard. A mistyped weight that looks like a real trend is the risk-analysis centrepiece, and usability engineering on the entry screen is where a notified body will push.

---

This is my reading of the regulation, not regulatory advice — Rule 11 borderline calls get litigated with notified bodies, so confirm the rationale with yours or a regulatory consultant before you build the technical file around it.

## Short answer

**Class I**, under **Rule 11, final limb** ("All other software is classified as class I") — assuming, as you stipulate, that qualification as a device is settled.

## The reasoning

**Rule 11 is the operative rule.** MDR Annex VIII, Chapter III, Section 6.3 is the only rule that speaks to standalone software, and Implementing Rule 3.3 confirms it applies in its own right here: the software is independent of any other device — it neither drives nor influences the use of the imaging equipment, so it does not inherit the modality's class.

Rule 11 then has three branches, and this product fails the first two:

**1. "Software intended to provide information which is used to take decisions with diagnosis or therapeutic purposes" (→ IIa/IIb/III).** The decisive question is whether the *software* provides the decision-relevant information, not whether decision-relevant information passes through it. Here, all clinical information is generated by the radiologist and fixed at signature. The software performs no action on the content: it does not analyse, derive, calculate, prioritise, flag, summarise or otherwise create anything a clinician did not already have. Reformatting layout and routing to an inbox is transport and presentation, not information provision in the Rule 11 sense. On the MDCG 2019-11 framing, this is the "storage, archival, communication, simple search" category of function — the same reasoning that normally *excludes* such software from qualification altogether also keeps it out of the first limb of Rule 11 if qualification is forced.

**2. "Software intended to monitor physiological processes" (→ IIa/IIb).** Plainly not — there is no physiological parameter being monitored.

**3. Residual limb → Class I.** That is where it lands.

No sub-class applies: it is not sterile (Is), has no measuring function (Im), and is not a reusable surgical instrument (Ir). So it is **plain Class I — self-certified, no notified body**, with conformity declared under Article 19 and technical documentation per Annexes II and III. You still owe the full Article 10 obligations: QMS, clinical evaluation (Annex XIV), UDI, PMS plan and PSUR-equivalent reporting, and Annex I GSPR 17 (electronic programmable systems — IT security, repeatability, reliability, verification/validation).

- **Any content transformation.** If the reformatting ever drops, truncates, reorders, abbreviates or selectively renders content — e.g. layout rules that push an incidental finding below a fold, or that separate the impression from a caveat — you are shaping what the GP reads, and the "we add nothing" argument collapses.
- **Any triage or prioritisation logic.** Flagging urgent reports, sorting the GP's inbox by acuity, or highlighting critical results is decision-support.
- **Marketing claims drifting ahead of the IFU.** Sales material promising "ensures GPs never miss a critical finding" is read as intended purpose by a competent authority, regardless of what the IFU says.

Note also that a notified body or authority taking a maximally literal reading of "provide information which is used to take decisions" could argue that the GP does in fact read this software's output and act on it, giving IIa. I think that reading is wrong — it proves too much, since it would capture every piece of hospital communication middleware — but if you want to reduce the argument surface, document in your technical file a bit-level or semantic-equivalence verification that report *content* is invariant across the transform, with only presentation changing. 2. **Rule 11, first indent** doesn't bite. It captures software that *provides information used to take decisions with a diagnostic or therapeutic purpose*. 3. **Rule 11, second indent** doesn't apply — no monitoring of physiological processes or parameters.

## Short answer

**Class I**, under the final catch-all sentence of Rule 11 in Annex VIII ("All other software is classified as class I"), applied via Implementing Rule 3.3 (standalone software is classified in its own right).

## Working through Annex VIII

**Implementing rules first**

- **Rule 3.3** — the software doesn't drive or influence the use of another device (it doesn't control the modality, the PACS acquisition, or a treatment device), so it is "independent of any other device" and classified in its own right rather than inheriting the class of anything else.
- **Rule 3.2 / 2.1** — classification follows the stated intended purpose: "to reformat and route finalised radiology reports to referring physicians." That purpose is about *transport and presentation*, not about generating, deriving, or interpreting clinical information.
- **Rule 3.5** — if several rules applied, the highest class wins. Here only Rule 11 bites (Rule 13, the catch-all for active devices, is displaced because Rule 11 is the specific software rule and has its own catch-all).

**Rule 11, indent by indent**

1. *"Software intended to provide information which is used to take decisions with diagnosis or therapeutic purposes" → IIa/IIb/III.* This is the one worth arguing about, and the answer is no. The diagnostic information is created and signed by the radiologist; the GP's decision rests on the radiologist's findings. Your software contributes no information of its own — it adds nothing, computes nothing, flags nothing, prioritises nothing. Under MDCG 2019-11 the trigger for this indent is software that *creates or derives* the information driving the decision, not software that moves an already-final human-authored conclusion from A to B. A fax machine in the path doesn't become the source of the diagnosis.
2. *Monitoring of physiological processes → IIa/IIb.* Plainly not applicable.
3. *"All other software is classified as class I."* This is where you land.

## The tension you should be aware of

You've told me qualification as a device is settled and not in question, so I've classified on that basis. But it's worth stating once, because it affects whether you're building the right file: MDCG 2019-11 §3.2 expressly says software whose action on data is limited to **storage, archival, communication, simple search, or lossless compression** is not MDSW at all. Pure reformatting plus routing, with no alteration of clinical content, sits very close to — arguably inside — that carve-out. If qualification was concluded on the basis that the output is "used for a medical purpose by the recipient," that reasoning is a known error mode; the medical purpose belongs to the report, not to the transport layer. If someone has decided otherwise for a defensible reason (e.g. the reformatting involves selective field mapping that could suppress content), that same reason is what a competent authority will probe, not the class.

Either way the class doesn't move: not a device, or a Class I device. There's no reading on these facts that gets you to IIa.

## Practical consequences of Class I

- Self-declaration — **no notified body** (it isn't sterile, measuring, or reusable surgical, so none of Is/Im/Ir apply).
- You still owe the full Annex I GSPRs, Annex II/III technical documentation, a risk management file (ISO 14971), a QMS per Article 10(9), clinical evaluation under Article 61 + Annex XIV, UDI assignment, EUDAMED registration, PMS plan and PSUR-equivalent per Article 85, and an EU declaration of conformity.
- No MDR transitional relief: Class I non-sterile/non-measuring devices have needed to be fully MDR-compliant since 26 May 2021.

## Where the real risk actually lives

Classification is the easy part. The failure modes that will hurt you here are **misrouting to the wrong GP** and **silent content loss during reformatting** (truncated impressions, dropped addenda, lost critical-finding flags, character-set mangling, missing "compared with prior" sections). Neither changes the Annex VIII class — classification runs on intended purpose, not on malfunction severity — but both need to be driven hard through your ISO 14971 file and your IEC 62304 software safety classification, where the harm from a dropped critical finding is genuinely serious. I'd expect a reviewer to spend all their time there and about ninety seconds on the class.

One caveat on national variation: a minority of competent authorities have historically read Rule 11's first indent more literally ("it provides information, that information is used for a diagnostic decision"). If you're placing this on the market across several member states, have the Rule 11 rationale written out explicitly in the technical documentation rather than leaving it implicit — it's a cheap defence against that reading.

There's no MDR class for it, because it isn't a medical device. A class only exists for products that first qualify as devices under Article 2(1) of Regulation (EU) 2017/745. The reasoning, in the order a regulator would apply it:

1. **Qualification first.** Art. 2(1) requires a medical intended purpose: diagnosis, prevention, monitoring, prediction, prognosis, treatment or alleviation of disease or injury. Recital 19 says explicitly that software intended for **lifestyle and well-being purposes** is not a medical device.
2. **Classification only if it passes step 1.** Since it doesn't, Annex VIII Rule 11 never applies.

MDCG 2019-11 is the guidance that walks this decision tree if anyone asks for a citation.

## The thing marketing actually needs to hear

**Don't put a class on the website.** There is no "MDR Class 0", no "MDR exempt" designation, and no "not applicable" badge — none of these are regulatory categories, and inventing one looks like a claim.

More importantly, stating a device class you don't hold cuts against you in both directions:

- Claiming **Class I** implies you've done the Class I obligations — technical documentation, Declaration of Conformity, EUDAMED registration, UDI, post-market surveillance, a CE mark. If you haven't, that's a false statement about a regulated product.
- Art. 7 MDR separately prohibits misleading claims about a product's status, function or performance. Asserting device status you don't have is the exact behaviour it targets.

The correct website statement is a plain negative, phrased as what the product *is*, not what regulation it escapes. Something like: *"[App] is a general wellness and lifestyle product. It is not a medical device and is not intended to diagnose, treat, cure or prevent any disease."* That sentence is also doing real work — it's part of the evidence of intended purpose that keeps you out of scope.

## What would flip you into scope

Your intended purpose is set by your claims, not your code. Marketing copy is exactly where products accidentally become medical devices. Watch for:

- Framing outputs as detecting or indicating a **condition** — "spot dehydration", "detect sleep apnoea", "your score may indicate burnout".
- **Risk or prevention** language — "reduce your risk of diabetes", "prevent cardiovascular disease".
- Positioning the score as something a user or clinician should **act on clinically**, or targeting it at a diagnosed patient population.
- **Monitoring physiological parameters** in a clinical sense, especially if you later add heart rate, SpO₂ or similar from a wearable.

## Answer: Class IIa, under Annex VIII Rule 11, first sub-paragraph

## How you get there

**Rule 11 is the only rule in play.** Implementation Rule 3.3 says software independent of any other device is classified in its own right — so you classify the DTx itself, not some host hardware. Rule 9 (active therapeutic devices administering or exchanging energy) doesn't bite: you administer instructions, not energy. Rules 10, 13, 14, 22 are all inapplicable. So Rule 11, and Implementation Rule 3.5 (highest applicable class) never gets exercised.

**The crux is your own framing.** You've written the intended purpose to say the software *is* the treatment and informs no one's decision. That's a real reading of Rule 11 — if the software neither provides information for a diagnostic/therapeutic decision nor monitors physiological processes, it drops to "all other software," Class I, self-certified. Rule 11 genuinely was drafted around information-providing software and handles direct digital therapy badly. But the argument is weaker than it looks:

- MDCG 2019-11 is explicit that the decision-taker under Rule 11 may be a healthcare professional, **the patient, or a lay person**. Removing the clinician doesn't remove the decision-maker; it relocates it to the patient.
- Your programme outputs patient-specific information that is acted on therapeutically: a computed sleep window ("in bed 00:40–05:30"), titration of that window week to week against diary data, stimulus-control instructions. The patient decides whether and how to act on each. That is information used to take a decision with a therapeutic purpose, on the ordinary reading.
- A notified body or competent authority reviewing a Class I self-declaration here would very likely reach IIa. A disputed self-declaration is not a document you fix in review — it's a market-withdrawal-grade problem, discovered after launch.

**Why it stops at IIa and doesn't escalate to IIb.** You need a positive, documented argument here, because sleep restriction is not a benign intervention and this is where a notified body will press. The escalation triggers are serious deterioration of health or a surgical intervention (IIb), or death or irreversible deterioration (III). The hazards worth naming in the rationale:

- Sleep restriction induces intentional daytime sleepiness → road-traffic and occupational accident risk.
- Sleep deprivation can precipitate mania in bipolar disorder, and lower seizure threshold in epilepsy.
- Insomnia treatment masking undiagnosed OSA → delayed diagnosis of the real condition.
- Untreated depression or active suicidality in the enrolled population.

Each of these is plausibly "serious deterioration" in the abstract. The reason they don't escalate the class is that they are controlled at the point of prescription by contraindications and exclusions in your intended purpose, not by the software's output — and the software's per-decision harm (one mistimed sleep window) is self-limiting and reversible. Write that argument down explicitly, with the exclusions mirrored in the IFU. Don't leave it implicit.

The second sub-paragraph of Rule 11 (monitoring physiological processes) is worth a sentence of dismissal too, if you ingest diary or wearable data: self-reported sleep diaries aren't monitoring of physiological processes, and sleep is not a vital physiological parameter whose variation creates immediate danger. Either way that limb lands on IIa, so it doesn't change the outcome.

## What IIa costs you

Notified body involvement, via Annex IX (QMS assessment plus technical documentation sampling) or Annex XI. Downstream: ISO 13485, IEC 62304 (expect software safety class B; C if your risk analysis takes the mania or driving hazards seriously), IEC 82304-1, ISO 14971, GSPR 17 for programmable systems, GSPR 22 for lay use, cybersecurity per MDCG 2019-16, UDI, PMS and PMCF.

Two things to plan around now rather than later:

- **Clinical evidence.** Equivalence under Article 61 is very hard to sustain for software — you cannot usually demonstrate technical equivalence to another vendor's programme, and you won't have access to their technical documentation. Budget for your own clinical investigation.
- **AI Act.** If any part of the programme is an AI system — adaptive titration, an ML-driven content selector, an NLP component in the cognitive restructuring exercises — then Class IIa plus a notified body route makes it high-risk under Article 6(1) of the AI Act, with its own conformity obligations layered on top. If you can keep the titration logic deterministic and rule-based, that is a materially cheaper product.

One note on terminology for the file: "prescription" isn't an MDR classification concept. It doesn't affect the class. It matters for your labelling, your lay-user GSPR obligations, and for reimbursement pathways — and it's load-bearing in the IIa-not-IIb argument above, since it's the prescriber who enforces the exclusions.

I'd flag that I'm giving you the classification reasoning, not a regulatory opinion you can file. Have your notified body or a regulatory consultant sign off on the Rule 11 rationale before it goes into the technical documentation.

## Bottom line: Class IIa, MDR Annex VIII Rule 11, first indent

Not Class I. The "it doesn't inform anyone's decision" argument is the one you'd most like to win, and it's the one a notified body will reject fastest.

## Why the Class I route fails

Rule 11's first limb catches "software intended to provide information which is used to take decisions with diagnosis or therapeutic purposes." Your instinct is that this presupposes a decision-maker downstream of the software, and that you've engineered that person out of the loop. But MDCG 2019-11 explicitly treats the *receiver* of the information as potentially the healthcare professional, the patient, or a lay person. The decision-maker doesn't have to be a clinician.

And your product unambiguously provides information to a patient who then acts on it. A sleep restriction schedule is an instruction: *be in bed 00:45–05:45 this week.* Stimulus control is an instruction: *get out of bed after 20 minutes awake.* The patient decides whether and how to follow it, and the therapeutic effect is mediated entirely through that decision. That is information used to take a therapeutic decision, on any reading a regulator will accept.

The deeper issue is that Rule 11 was drafted on the assumption that software *informs* therapy rather than *constitutes* it. There is no rule in Annex VIII that says "software that is itself the treatment." That gap is real and well recognised, but it resolves against you: regulators close it by reading the first limb of Rule 11 broadly, not by dropping therapeutic software into the Class I residual bucket. "All other software is Class I" is a residual category for things like generic viewers, EHR data storage, and administrative tooling — arguing a prescription therapeutic into it invites an Article 94 problem later, and self-certification means nobody catches the error until it's expensive.

One thing that may be confusing your market scan: several CBT-I products (Sleepio, some German DiGAs) were legitimately Class I under MDD Rule 12, and under the UK's still-MDD-based regime some still carry Class I marking. The Rule 11 rewrite is precisely what up-classified that whole cohort — it's the single most disruptive change MDR made to the DiGA sector. Competitor labelling from the MDD era is not evidence for your MDR position.

## Why it stops at IIa and doesn't go to IIb

Escalation to IIb requires that the decisions driven by the software may cause serious deterioration of health or a surgical intervention. There is a genuine argument here, and you should expect to have it, because sleep restriction works by deliberately inducing acute sleep deprivation. The credible harm pathways:

- **Daytime somnolence and psychomotor impairment** in weeks 1–3, with a documented drowsy-driving signal. An MVA is serious deterioration.
- **Bipolar disorder** — sleep deprivation can precipitate mania or hypomania. This is the sharpest one.
- **Seizure disorders** — lowered seizure threshold.
- **Untreated OSA**, where the programme delays diagnosis of the actual condition.
- **Comorbid depression with suicidality**, where insomnia is itself a risk factor.

The reason this still lands at IIa rather than IIb is that Rule 11's escalation test looks at the *expected* impact of decisions the software is intended to drive, in the intended population, not at worst-case misuse in contraindicated patients. Provided your intended purpose and IFU scope the population to adults with chronic insomnia and exclude the contraindicated groups, and provided prescription gating puts a clinician between the product and the patient at intake, the residual pathways are non-serious in the ordinary case.

That defence is contingent, though. Three things would move you to IIb, and they're worth treating as design constraints rather than paperwork:

1. **No safety floor on the prescribed sleep window.** An algorithm that can compute a 4-hour or shorter time-in-bed, or that can ratchet down without bound on sparse or implausible diary data, produces severe iatrogenic deprivation directly. Hard floor (typically 5h, some protocols 5.5h), plus sanity checks on diary input.
2. **Broadening the population** to adolescents, or to psychiatric comorbidity as an indication rather than an exclusion.
3. **Dropping the prescription requirement** or moving to OTC/direct-to-consumer, which removes the clinician screen you're relying on.

## Rules to address and dismiss in the rationale

- **Rule 11 second limb (monitoring physiological processes):** doesn't bite. Self-reported sleep diaries aren't sensor-based monitoring of a physiological parameter. Note that even if you later add actigraphy or wearable integration, sleep is not a vital physiological parameter whose variation causes immediate danger — you'd stay at IIa. Useful to state now so a roadmap feature doesn't reopen the classification.
- **Rule 22 (active therapeutic device with integrated diagnostic function, closed-loop):** I'd pre-empt this one explicitly. Your diary-in/schedule-out titration loop is superficially closed-loop, and Annex VIII §3.5 makes the strictest applicable rule govern. The answer is that Rule 22 sits in the active-device chapter and targets devices administering or exchanging energy or substances — AEDs, closed-loop insulin. It is not applied to standalone MDSW. But write the paragraph; if a reviewer raises it and you have no prepared answer, it costs you weeks.

## What Class IIa actually commits you to

- Notified body involvement — Annex IX QMS plus technical documentation assessment on a sampling basis, or Annex XI Part A. Budget the lead time; NB capacity is still the binding constraint on DTx timelines.
- ISO 13485, ISO 14971, IEC 62366-1, IEC 62304.
- **Watch the IEC 62304 software safety class — this is the trap.** Class IIa under MDR does not imply Class B under 62304; the two are assigned on different logic. 62304 §4.3 assigns the class on severity of harm *before* software-internal risk controls, crediting only controls external to the software system. Your bipolar and seizure pathways are serious-injury, and the controls you're crediting (prescription screening, IFU warnings) are external — which gets you to B, but the argument is thinner than teams expect. I'd use §4.3 segregation: hold the sleep-window scheduling engine to the higher bar and let content delivery sit lower, rather than arguing a blanket B across the whole system. If the scheduling engine has no architecturally enforced floor, expect to defend C.
- **Clinical evaluation:** a clinical investigation isn't mandatory at IIa (Article 61(4) mandates it only for Class III and implantables), but the published CBT-I evidence base is evidence for the *therapy*, not for *your device*, and equivalence to another DTx is very hard to argue on software. Plan for your own RCT. Payer routes — DiGA in particular — will require it regardless of what the NB accepts.

## What I'd nail down before writing the rationale

Whether "no clinician in the loop" extends to intake. If a prescriber screens for bipolar disorder, epilepsy, OSA and suicidality before the patient ever opens the app, your IIa position is comfortable. If the prescription is a formality and screening happens inside the software, you're relying on your own device to exclude the patients whose harm pathway drives the classification — which is circular, and is where a reviewer will push.

Final call sits with your notified body, and the Rule 11/Rule 22 framing you hand them shapes how hard they push.

## Bottom line

**Class I**, under the final limb of Rule 11 (Annex VIII, MDR 2017/745) — "all other software." But this is the contested flavour of Class I, and the argument needs to be built deliberately rather than assumed.

## The reasoning chain

**Implementing rule 3.3** — the software is independent of any other device, so it's classified in its own right. No inheritance from hardware.

**Rule 9 doesn't bite.** People reach for it because the device is therapeutic, but Rule 9 is confined to active therapeutic devices *intended to administer or exchange energy*. A CBT-I programme administers instructions, not energy.

**So Rule 11 governs**, and it has three outcomes:
- *Limb 1* — information used to take decisions with diagnostic or therapeutic purposes → IIa, escalating to IIb (serious deterioration / surgical intervention) or III (death / irreversible deterioration).
- *Limb 2* — monitoring physiological processes → IIa, or IIb for vital parameters where variation creates immediate danger.
- *Neither* → Class I.

On your facts — the software *is* the intervention, nothing is fed to a clinician, no decision support — you land on the third branch. The MDCG 2019-11 decision tree supports this, and there's market precedent: somnio and Sleepio were both CE-marked Class I, and the German DiGA register accepts Class I and IIa.

## Where the exposure actually is

Your framing — "it doesn't feed information to anyone to decide anything" — is the right framing, but it has one weak joint. **MDCG 2019-11 counts patients and lay persons among those who "take decisions."** Your sleep restriction module computes an individualised time-in-bed window from the patient's diary data, and the patient then acts on it. A notified body or competent authority can characterise that as information driving a therapeutic decision → IIa. Nothing in the rule text forecloses that reading, and scrutiny of Rule 11 self-certification has tightened since the early DTx approvals.

The IIb argument (sleep restriction → daytime somnolence → road traffic accident, or worsening insomnia → depression/suicidality) exists but is a stretch. Treat IIa as the realistic downside case.

**The most likely thing to break your Class I position is an adjacent feature, not the core programme.** Implementing rule 3.5 means the strictest applicable rule sets the class for the whole device. So watch for:
- ISI or PSQI scoring that surfaces a severity or diagnostic output
- OSA screening (STOP-BANG or similar) used to triage
- a suicidality flag that escalates to a clinician — this is the textbook Rule 11 limb 1 trigger, and it's exactly the kind of safety feature a good risk file pushes you toward
- wearable or diary-derived physiological monitoring, which is limb 2

If any of those ship in the same device, you're IIa regardless of how the core programme is characterised.

## What to do with this

Align the intended purpose wording with the classification: "delivers cognitive behavioural therapy" is right; anything phrased as *providing recommendations, advice, or information to the patient* hands the opposing reading to the assessor. Keep the sleep window framed as a prescribed schedule the programme sets, not a recommendation the patient evaluates.

Write the Rule 11 rationale into the technical documentation explicitly, citing MDCG 2019-11 and naming the patient-as-decision-maker counterargument and why you reject it. An assessor who finds you already considered it is in a different posture than one who thinks you missed it.

Worth a deliberate decision rather than a default: **taking IIa voluntarily.** It costs a notified body (Annex IX Ch. I + III, QMS plus tech doc assessment on a sampling basis), time and money. It buys you immunity from mid-lifecycle reclassification, freedom to add the screening and safety features above, and a better position with payers and procurement in several markets.

## If Class I holds, downstream

Article 52(7) self-declaration, no notified body (software isn't sterile, measuring, or reusable surgical). Annex II/III technical documentation, EUDAMED registration and SRN, PRRC under Article 15, UDI. PMS report under Article 85 — no PSUR obligation, that starts at IIa. Clinical evaluation under Article 61 and Annex XIV: for a device claiming to *treat*, plan on your own clinical investigation; the equivalence route is not realistically available to you. Standards: IEC 62304, IEC 82304-1, ISO 14971, ISO 13485, ISO 14155 for the trial, MDCG 2019-16 for cybersecurity.

Risk file items that also strengthen the classification story: exclusion criteria (untreated OSA, bipolar disorder, seizure disorders, shift workers), a hard floor on prescribed time-in-bed, and daytime-sleepiness/driving warnings during the restriction phase.

One caveat worth naming: classification is harmonised across the EU, but the Rule 11 judgement here is genuinely contested, so confirm the position with your notified body or a competent authority before you build the regulatory strategy on it. If the UK is in scope, that's a separate analysis under UK MDR 2002 — the old MDD rules, which get you to Class I more comfortably.

Two things are tangled in the question, and the answer turns on separating them.

## 1. This is a qualification question, not a classification one

You're asking whether it's Medical Device Software at all. That's MDR **Art. 2(1)** — does the software have a medical purpose within the definition. The Annex VIII machinery I have verified (implementing rules 3.1–3.7, Rule 11) only runs *after* qualification is established. It assumes you already have a device and tells you which class it is. So I can't answer "is it MDSW" from Annex VIII, and Rule 11 producing "class I" is not the same statement as "not a device."

Practically: if it isn't a device, there's no class and no conformity route. If it is, then we run 3.3 → Rule 11, and on your description it would land in limb 3 (class I) — but don't build on that, because the interesting risk for you is entirely on the qualification side.

## 2. The "simple search" position — and why I won't hand it to you as authority

The distinction you're describing is real and it lives in **MDCG 2019-11**, *Guidance on Qualification and Classification of Software in Regulation (EU) 2017/745 – MDR and Regulation (EU) 2017/746 – IVDR* (there is a Rev. 1; check which revision is current before citing). Its decision logic turns on whether the software performs **an action on data beyond storage, archival, communication, lossless compression, or simple search** — with "simple search" meaning retrieval of records by matching record metadata against search criteria. Software doing only that is not MDSW. Software that creates or modifies medical information, or interprets it to support a clinical decision, is.

Three caveats on that, and they matter:

- **It's guidance, not the regulation.** MDCG documents are Commission/Medical Device Coordination Group guidance and are not legally binding. They carry real weight with notified bodies and competent authorities, but "the official position" is guidance-strength, not law-strength. The binding text is Art. 2(1).
- **I'm quoting that from recollection, not from a verified source.** My skill's reference file deliberately excludes MDCG 2019-11, and I couldn't retrieve the document just now — web access is blocked in this session. Get the PDF from the Commission's health/medical-devices guidance page and read the passage yourself before it goes in a technical file or a regulatory argument. Enable web access and I'll pull the verbatim text and section number.

## 3. Where I'd actually push back on "pure retrieval"

The carve-out is narrower than it sounds, and the phrase "no ranking by clinical relevance" is doing a lot of work in your description. Things that would move this out of "simple search":

- **What the matching runs on.** "Matching record metadata against search criteria" is the guidance's framing. If retrieval is keyword/metadata matching, you're comfortably inside. If it's semantic or embedding-based retrieval, you're arguably performing an action on the content rather than matching metadata — even with no explicit score shown to the clinician. Relevance ordering is still ordering.
- **Whether the criteria embed clinical logic.** Searching by document title, date, author, department: fine. Surfacing documents *because they apply to this patient's condition* is interpretation wearing a search interface, regardless of whether you call the output a ranking.
- **What's in the library.** A library of hospital policies, SOPs and guidelines points away from a medical purpose entirely. A library of patient records points toward one, and the analysis gets harder.

## What I'd put in front of your regulatory lead

The Art. 2(1) call with the intended purpose exactly as written; the retrieval mechanism (metadata match vs. semantic); and the contents of the library. Those three settle it. I'm a structured first pass, not a regulatory opinion — this should be confirmed by your regulatory lead or notified body.

As described, no — pure retrieval is outside MDSW. But the exemption is narrower than it sounds, and the phrase "returns matching documents" is doing more work in your sentence than the guidance will let it.

## The authority

**MDR Art. 2(1) + Recital 19** — software is a device in its own right when the manufacturer specifically intends it for a medical purpose. Intended purpose, not architecture, is the trigger.

**MDCG 2019-11**, *Guidance on Qualification and Classification of Software in Regulation (EU) 2017/745 – MDR and Regulation (EU) 2017/746 – IVDR*. This is the operative text and the only place "simple search" is defined.

- **Decision Step 3** of the qualification flowchart: software that performs no action on data, or an action **limited to storage, archival, communication, "simple search" or lossless compression**, is not MDSW.
- **The defining footnote** — the sentence you actually want to quote: simple search means retrieval of records by matching record metadata against record metadata, or retrieval of records by matching text. And the carve-out: simple search **does not** include software providing *interpretative* search results, e.g. to identify, develop or provide recommendations regarding matching medical information for individual patients.
- **Step 4** asks whether the action is for the benefit of *individual patients*. A library of hospital guidelines/SOPs/policies is reference material, not patient-specific processing — a second independent reason you sit outside. MDCG's examples section treats hospital information systems the same way.

That footnote *is* the official position on "simple search vs. search that adds value." The line is not "is the output clinically useful" — it's **literal matching vs. interpretation**.

## Where your description is fragile

Three things I'd press on, because they're where this qualification usually breaks:

1. **Matching *how*.** Keyword, boolean, exact-text, metadata filters — clearly simple search. Embeddings, semantic similarity, or LLM query expansion — much harder to defend, because you're operating on the *meaning* of a clinical query, which is what "interpretative" is aimed at.
2. **"No ranking" may not survive contact with the implementation.** Vector retrieval *is* ranking by similarity; not displaying the score doesn't remove the action. MDCG assesses what the software does to the data, not what the UI shows. Even BM25/TF-IDF ordering is grey — defensible as lexical matching, weaker if the UI says "best match."
3. **Intended purpose is set by you, in the IFU and the marketing** (MDR Art. 2(12)). If anything customer-facing says "finds the right protocol for your patient," you've claimed a medical purpose and the clean retrieval architecture won't save you.

Worth knowing the stake: if it *did* qualify, Rule 11 of Annex VIII puts software informing diagnostic or therapeutic decisions at Class IIa minimum. That's why this is worth documenting properly rather than concluding informally.

If the hospital is building this itself rather than buying it, also look at the Art. 5(5) health institution exemption — different route to the same place, with its own conditions.

## Other jurisdictions, briefly

- **UK:** MHRA's *Medical device stand-alone software including apps* guidance mirrors the same reasoning under the UK MDR 2002. MHRA's software/AI reform programme has been moving — check current status.
- **US:** FD&C Act §520(o)(1) (21 U.S.C. 360j(o)), from the 21st Century Cures Act — (A) administrative support, (D) transfer/store/display, (E) CDS. Read FDA's **September 2022 final CDS guidance**; it's directly on point for you because FDA treats *prioritised or ranked* outputs as more device-like, on the theory that the clinician can't independently review the basis. FDA is stricter on ranking than MDCG is.

## What I'd actually do

Write the qualification decision down now, against each MDCG step, while the answer is easy. Freeze the intended purpose statement. Then set a change-control trigger: **any** move to semantic/vector retrieval, any surfaced relevance score, any injection of patient context into the query re-opens qualification from Step 3. That's the transition that catches teams out — the product drifts into MDSW one sprint at a time and nobody re-runs the assessment.

Not regulatory advice — get your RA function or a notified body to sign the rationale.
