## Short answer

On your description — retrieval only, no scoring, no clinical relevance ranking, no interpretation — it is **not** Medical Device Software in the EU/UK, and not a device in the US. "Simple search" is a named, explicit carve-out, not a judgement call you have to argue from first principles.

## EU — the authority

**MDCG 2019-11**, *Guidance on Qualification and Classification of Software in Regulation (EU) 2017/745 – MDR and Regulation (EU) 2017/746 – IVDR*. This is the one you cite.

The decision tree (Figure 1) has a step that asks, in effect: *is the software performing an action on data beyond storage, archival, communication, simple search or lossless compression?* If no → it is not MDSW, and you stop there. Pure retrieval fails that step.

The accompanying footnote is the operative text, and it draws exactly the line you're asking about:

> "Simple search" refers to the retrieval of records by matching record metadata against record search criteria... It does not cover software which provides interpretative search results, e.g. to identify medical findings in health records or to interpret patient medical findings.

So the official distinction is **matching vs. interpreting** — not "basic vs. sophisticated," and not how good the search engine is.

Supporting authority:
- **MDR Art. 2(1)** — software is a device only where it has an *intended medical purpose* assigned by the manufacturer. Qualification turns on your claimed intended purpose, not on the technology.
- **MDR Recital 19** — software in its own right qualifies only when specifically intended for a medical purpose; general-purpose software used in a healthcare setting does not.
- **MDR Annex VIII, Rule 11** — this is the stake. If it *did* qualify, software providing information used to take diagnostic or therapeutic decisions is **Class IIa minimum**, escalating to IIb/III on harm severity. There is no Class I landing spot. That's why the qualification step is where the whole argument lives.

**UK:** MHRA's guidance *Medical device stand-alone software including apps (including IVDMDs)* takes the same position and is aligned with MDCG 2019-11 on this point. The UK MDR 2002 definition still governs pending reform.

## US — the authority

**FD&C Act § 520(o)(1)**, inserted by § 3060 of the **21st Century Cures Act (2016)**, statutorily removes several software functions from the device definition. Your tool most plausibly sits in:

- **§ 520(o)(1)(A)** — administrative support of a healthcare facility;
- **§ 520(o)(1)(D)** — transferring, storing, converting formats, or displaying data — **expressly conditioned on the software not being intended to interpret or analyse** that data;
- **§ 520(o)(1)(C)** — serving as electronic patient records, if the library is patient-record content.

FDA's implementing guidances: *Changes to Existing Medical Software Policies Resulting from Section 3060 of the 21st Century Cures Act* (final, Sept 2022) and *Clinical Decision Support Software* (final, Sept 2022).

## The "adds value" line — where it actually breaks

This is the part worth your attention, because the EU and US both put the tripwire earlier than people expect:

1. **Ranking by clinical relevance is the classic trigger.** FDA's 2022 CDS guidance is explicit and notably narrow here: software that outputs a *prioritised or ranked list* of options is treated as providing a specific diagnostic or treatment output, failing the CDS exclusion criteria and landing as a device. Ranking is not a neutral UI nicety to a regulator.
2. **Lexical/semantic relevance ordering ≠ clinical relevance ordering.** Ordering by BM25 or embedding similarity to the *query string* is still matching. Ordering by inferred fit to *this patient* is interpretation. If your engine ranks at all, document which one it is — because in practice every search engine orders results, and "no ranking" will not survive a reviewer opening the code.
3. **Snippets, summaries, or RAG-style generated answers over the retrieved documents** — that is an action on data beyond retrieval. Adding a generated answer layer on top of this tool would very likely flip it to MDSW and straight into Rule 11 Class IIa. Worth deciding now, before someone ships it as a "small feature."
4. **Auto-querying from patient context** (pulling problem list or labs from the EHR to build the query) pushes toward CDS in both jurisdictions.
5. **Suppressing results as "not relevant"** is a filtering judgement, and is harder to defend than returning an over-inclusive set.
6. **Your claims bind you.** "Search the document library" is safe. "Find the right protocol for your patient" assigns a medical purpose under MDR Art. 2(1) and can qualify the product on marketing copy alone, regardless of what the code does.

## Two practical points

**Write the rationale down.** The burden of demonstrating non-qualification sits with you. A short file holding the intended purpose statement, the MDCG 2019-11 decision-tree walkthrough, and an explicit "what would change this" list is the artefact an auditor or a hospital's procurement team will ask for.

**Not a medical device ≠ unregulated.** If you're deploying into the NHS in England, **DCB0129** (clinical risk management for health IT manufacturers) applies to health software irrespective of medical device status, and DTAC will likely be asked for. Plus GDPR/UK GDPR on the underlying records.

One thing I'd need to size the answer properly: which market is this for — EU, UK, US, or all three? The conclusion is the same in each, but the documentation you'd produce differs.

## Short answer

On the facts as you've stated them — no. Pure retrieval falls outside Medical Device Software via an explicit carve-out. But the carve-out is narrower than "we don't rank by clinical relevance," and the phrase "document library" is doing a lot of unexamined work.

## The authority

**Primary law:** Regulation (EU) 2017/745 (MDR), Art. 2(1) — software qualifies as a medical device where it has a medical intended purpose. Recital 19 confirms software in its own right is a device when it has such a purpose. Art. 2(12) defines "intended purpose" by reference to *the manufacturer's* claims (labelling, IFU, marketing) — which matters below.

**The operative guidance:** **MDCG 2019-11**, *Guidance on Qualification and Classification of Software in Regulation (EU) 2017/745 – MDR and Regulation (EU) 2017/746 – IVDR*. Current revision is **Rev.1, March 2023**.

**The mechanism** is the qualification decision tree in Figure 1. The relevant step asks whether the software performs an action on data **other than** storage, archival, communication, **"simple search"**, or lossless compression. If it does not, the analysis stops — it is not MDSW.

**The definition you want** is the note attached to that step. In substance: *"simple search" means retrieval of records by matching record metadata against record search criteria* — and the example given is literally **library functions**. It then excludes software providing **interpretative** search results, with examples along the lines of identifying medical findings in health records, analysis of medical images, or searching for potential contraindications.

**Lineage, if anyone tells you this is a novel MDR-era reading:** the same language and the same decision step appear in **MEDDEV 2.1/6** (rev. July 2016), the pre-MDR guideline. This interpretation is over a decade old and survived the MDR transition intact.

## The actual dividing line — and why it isn't "adds value"

The official test is **not** whether the search is clinically useful. Useful is fine. The test is whether the software **performs an action on the data**. MDCG's positive limb is that software intended to *process, analyse, create or modify* medical information is MDSW where that creation or modification is governed by a medical intended purpose.

Metadata matching creates no new information — the clinician gets back exactly the records that already existed. Once the software generates something that wasn't in the library (a relevance score, a ranking, a summary, an extracted snippet, a flag), it has created information, and you move to the next decision step (is the action for the benefit of an individual patient?) — at which point you are very likely MDSW.

## Where I think your position is weaker than you're assuming

1. **"Metadata" is the load-bearing word, not "no ranking."** If your product is semantic or embedding-based search over document *content* — i.e. anything RAG-shaped — that is not matching metadata against search criteria. It is analysis of the content to infer meaning. The carve-out is on materially weaker ground there, and this is the first thing a notified body will probe. Plain lexical matching on titles, codes, dates, and tags is squarely inside the carve-out; vector similarity over clinical text is a genuine argument, not a settled one.
2. **Snippets and previews.** Generating an extract "responsive to the query" is creating information. Returning the whole document is safer than returning the relevant paragraph.
3. **Your own marketing can qualify you.** Under Art. 2(12), qualification follows the stated intended purpose. "Helps clinicians find the right guideline for this patient" claims a medical purpose no matter how dumb your retrieval is. Police the claims as tightly as you police the architecture.
4. **What's actually in the library?** If it holds institutional documents — policies, protocols, guidelines, SOPs — you get a *second, independent* reason to be out: the action isn't for the benefit of an individual patient. If it holds patient records, you're relying on the simple-search carve-out alone, with no fallback.
5. **Accessory status.** Art. 2(2) — if the tool is intended specifically to enable or assist another device, it can be regulated as an accessory even while not being a device in its own right.

And the stakes if you cross the line: **Rule 11, Annex VIII** puts software providing information used for diagnostic or therapeutic decisions at **Class IIa minimum**, which means notified body involvement. That's why the ranking question is worth getting right up front rather than at audit.

## Other jurisdictions, briefly

- **UK:** MHRA guidance *Medical device stand-alone software including apps* mirrors the MEDDEV/MDCG decision tree; UK MDR 2002 remains in force.
- **US:** different route entirely. FD&C Act **§520(o)**, inserted by **§3060 of the 21st Century Cures Act (2016)**, excludes software for administrative support of a healthcare facility (§520(o)(1)(A)) and for maintaining or transferring health records (§520(o)(1)(C)). Retrieval that starts recommending gets picked up by FDA's **Clinical Decision Support Software** final guidance (September 2022), which reads the CDS exemption criteria narrowly — patient-specific outputs where the clinician can't independently review the basis are devices.

## What I'd do next

Write the "no action on data" conclusion down as a formal qualification rationale referencing MDCG 2019-11 Figure 1 and the simple-search note, and — the part teams skip — add a **design constraint to your requirements** stating that the retrieval layer performs metadata matching only and returns unmodified documents. That's what converts a defensible reading into evidence, and it's what stops a well-meaning engineer from shipping relevance ranking in a sprint eighteen months from now and silently making you a Class IIa manufacturer.
